To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the infection of mycoplasma free L-cell cultures with influenza viruses did not result in the formation of infectious viral particles, but some changes persisted on subcultivation.

L-cell cultures infected either with avian influenza viruses or with human influenza virus did not produce infectious virions, but some changes in the infected cultures were demonstrated which persisted on subculture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the changes in the L-cells after infection by influenza viruses.
the alteration of L-cell cultures after infection with influenza viruses, which was demonstrated by direct count.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the influenza viruses did not reproduce in L-cells.
the infection of the L-cells with influenza viruses A0 and FPV did not result in the production of infectious virus.
the influenza viruses did not multiply in the L-cells, although the adsorbtion of the viruses was very high.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
L-cells are susceptible to influenza viruses, but the infection does not lead to the synthesis of infectious virions.
the L-cell culture infected by influenza viruses is a good model for studying the synthesis of viral antigens and the mechanism of the CPE.
L-cell cultures are resistant to influenza viruses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the L-cells infected by influenza viruses were not able to reproduce infectious virions, but they were able to produce noninfectious antigens.
the infected L-cells were able to synthesize viral antigens, which could be found by immunofluorescent tests with the use of specific antibodies.
L-cells infected with FPV or influenza viruses A0 produced some alterations which were maintained on subcultures and which could be used as an indicator of viral contamination.
